implementation_notes: Java ships the pattern: extend RecursiveTask<T> (result) or RecursiveAction (void), split until a threshold in compute(), fork one subtask, compute the other in the current thread and join - the ForkJoinPool's workers steal from each other's deques, and invokeAll joins in a helping manner so the caller never idles. The static commonPool() backs tasks not submitted to a specific pool (and both Arrays.parallelSort and parallel streams); submit/invoke from outside a computation, and use a dedicated pool only when isolation or a specific parallelism level is required. Since the classic structure IS the API, library support here means: use RecursiveTask instead of hand-rolled deques.
pitfalls: Common-pool starvation: blocking, I/O or sleeping inside a task occupies workers that every other parallel stream shares; use ForkJoinPool.managedBlock for unavoidable blocking or a dedicated pool.
Forking both halves and then joining both immediately leaves the parent with nothing to do - fork one side and compute the other (invokeAll is the exception, it helps while joining).
Task state must not rely on ThreadLocal or shared mutable fields: the executing worker is generally not the submitting thread, and ForkJoinTask failures are rethrown from join()/invoke().

variants.name: Parallel streams on the common pool (Java 8)
variants.implementation_notes: Parallel streams are fork/join with the decomposition hidden: a spliterator splits the source, the pipeline stages run as ForkJoinTasks in the common pool and the terminal operation joins the results. Use them for uniform data-parallel bulk operations over index-friendly collections (arrays, ArrayLists, ranges) where map/filter/reduce expresses the whole computation; keep the RecursiveTask form for irregular recursion - uneven trees, pruning, custom combine steps and threshold logic the stream API cannot express.
variants.code_sketch:
long total = LongStream.range(0, a.length)   // splittable range source
        .parallel()                          // fork via common pool
        .map(i -> work(a[(int) i]))
        .sum();                              // join + combine
pitfalls: All parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool: one blocking stage starves every other parallel stream in the JVM.
forEach is unordered and side effects are unsafe; use forEachOrdered or collect for deterministic results.
Poorly splittable sources (LinkedList, iterators, I/O-backed streams) parallelize badly - the splitting overhead can exceed the work.
